what: Etsy runs an online marketplace for handmade, custom and vintage goods. It does not hold inventory; independent sellers list items and Etsy takes a cut of each sale plus fees for payments and advertising. It also owns Depop, a resale app popular with younger shoppers.
customers: Shoppers looking for something not mass-produced, and the millions of small sellers who list on the platform and pay its fees.
money: Transaction fees, listing fees and payment processing on goods sold.
Seller advertising, promoted listings and shipping label sales.
moat: The marketplace is self-reinforcing: buyers come because of the breadth of unusual items, and sellers come because the buyers are there. No competitor has assembled a comparable catalogue of handmade and vintage goods, and the brand itself signals what the site is for.
risks: Gross merchandise sales have been flat to declining, which is the measure that matters most for a marketplace, and revenue has only grown because Etsy raised fees.
Raising take rates on sellers can work for a while, but it also pushes sellers toward building their own shops on Shopify.
Debt of $3.0B against $1.6B of cash is unusually high for a marketplace with no inventory.
Discretionary spending on non-essential gifts and decor is among the first things consumers cut.
Search traffic from Google is an important acquisition channel, and algorithm changes can cut it without warning.
opportunities: Free cash flow of roughly $592.5M against a $6.8B market value is a strong yield, and the business needs almost no capital.
The shares trade at about 21 times earnings and 11.5 times free cash flow.
Depop is growing in resale, a category expanding faster than the core marketplace.
Twenty-seven analysts average a $98.48 target, about 25% above the current price.
watch: Gross merchandise sales, not revenue. Fee increases can mask a shrinking marketplace for several years; the value of goods sold through the platform is the honest measure of whether Etsy is still growing.
